title: What is a ratio? One cup of juice, three cups of water
description: Your picnic drink has a 1:3 ratio. Find out what those numbers compare, why the total is four parts, and how to make a bigger batch.

hub.name: Fractions, one piece at a time

cover.alt: Four equal-sized glasses filled to the same height: one orange juice and three clear water
cover.credit: AI-generated cover image created for BrainiLab.

practice: Try a few quick calculations in Math Rush after checking the proportions.

sections.title: A picnic drink with two numbers
sections.html:
A ratio compares two quantities in a stated order. If you mix one cup of juice with three cups of water, the juice-to-water ratio is 1:3. Read it as “one to three”. OpenStax explains this notation.

Imagine a picnic where you are in charge of the drinks. Use the same cup for both ingredients. One tiny juice measure beside three enormous water mugs would make a very different drink—and some disappointed guests.

sections.title: Why one to three makes four parts
sections.html:
There are four equal measures altogether: one juice plus three water. Juice makes up 1/4 of the total measured amount, or 25%. It does not make up 1/3 of the whole.

The difference is what you compare. 1:3 compares juice with water; 1/4 compares juice with the whole. NRICH explores this distinction through drink mixtures. The numbers become clearer when you name both sides.

sections.title: More guests, same mixture
sections.html:
For a larger batch, use two cups of juice and six cups of water. The ratio 2:6 has the same proportions as 1:3: you doubled both quantities.

Now juice accounts for 2/8 of the measured total, still 1/4. That is the idea behind equivalent fractions. Doubling only the water would change the mixture. Your jug may be fuller, but you have not preserved the recipe.

sections.title: Which ingredient comes first?
sections.html:
Order matters. For this mixture, water to juice is 3:1, the reverse of juice to water.

Here is one final ratio example. For 600 mL of ingredients measured before mixing, split the total into four equal shares: 600 ÷ 4 = 150 mL. Use 150 mL of juice and 450 mL of water.

Before calculating, ask two small questions: “What am I comparing?” and “Are the measures the same size?” They save a surprising amount of confusion—and watery picnic drinks.

questions.prompt: A juice-to-water ratio is 1:3, using equal-sized measures. How many measures are there altogether?
questions.explanation: One juice measure plus three water measures makes four measures. Juice is one quarter of that total.

questions.prompt: Which juice-to-water ratio keeps the same proportions as 1:3?
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers by two: 1:3 becomes 2:6. Doubling just one quantity changes the proportions.

questions.prompt: You need 600 mL of measured ingredients at a juice-to-water ratio of 1:3. How much juice do you measure?
questions.explanation: There are four shares. Each is 600 ÷ 4 = 150 mL; juice uses one share and water uses three.
